subtitle: A comprehensive reference for consistent Internet security terminology

tldr.problem: Internet standards documents (RFCs) used inconsistent, unclear, or misleading security terminology, making standards harder to understand and implement correctly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2828 provides a comprehensive glossary of 1,000+ security terms with definitions marked as recommended (for Internet use) or deprecated, along with explanations of why certain terms should or should not be used.
tldr.outcome: The RFC established a shared vocabulary to improve clarity and consistency in Internet security standards, though it was replaced by RFC 4949 with expanded coverage.

facts.label: Page count
facts.value: 212 (191 pages of definitions, 13 pages of references)

today: RFC 2828 was obsoleted by RFC 4949 in August 2007, which expanded the glossary with terms reflecting advances in cryptography and protocols since 2000. However, RFC 2828 remains a foundational reference for understanding how the Internet security community defined terminology at the start of the twenty-first century, and its principles—that consistent, clear, and neutral language is essential for standards—remain relevant today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2828 is a comprehensive glossary of security-related terminology designed to improve the clarity and consistency of Internet Standards documents (ISDs). The RFC addresses a fundamental problem: the Internet security community was using the same terms in different ways, or using different terms for the same concept, making standards documents confusing and error-prone.

The glossary contains abbreviations, definitions, explanations, and recommendations for nearly 1,000 security terms. It is not itself an Internet standard; rather, it is an informational document that supports the goals of the Internet Standards Process by promoting clear documentation, technical excellence, and openness to competing security technologies.
sections.eli5: This is a rulebook for security writers. It says which security words to use, which to avoid, and why each word matters in Internet standards.

sections.title: Scope and Coverage
sections.content:
The glossary covers security terminology used in the Internet Standards Process and related Internet documents. It includes 1,000+ entries organized alphabetically, covering terms related to authentication, cryptography, access control, key management, protocols, attacks, and security models.

The glossary is self-contained in a technical sense: every abbreviation or term mentioned in a definition is itself defined in the glossary. This means a reader unfamiliar with security terminology can start with almost any term and trace its meaning through cross-references. Terms are divided into categories: some are core Internet security concepts (marked I), others are well-established non-Internet concepts (N), definitions needed for context but not recommended for use (O), and deprecated terms that should be avoided (D).
sections.eli5: The glossary covers all the security words used in Internet standards: how to talk about locks and keys, attacks and defenses, and who is allowed to do what on a computer network.

sections.title: How Terms Are Classified
sections.content:
RFC 2828 marks each definition with letters that indicate how to use it in Internet standards documents. I-marked definitions (Recommended, Internet basis) are the first choice for ISDs and typically describe concepts that originated in Internet standards or are generic enough that the RFC can define them without conflicting with non-Internet authorities. N-marked definitions (Recommended, Non-Internet basis) are the first choice when a term is used, but the term comes from another standards body (such as OSI, X.509, or U.S. government standards).

O-marked definitions (Other) describe terms that are not recommended as a first choice for ISDs. These might be non-Internet definitions that need clarification, or definitions needed for context when discussing non-Internet technologies. D-marked definitions (Deprecated) warn that a term SHOULD NOT be used in ISDs because it is ambiguous, misleading, or conflicts with other established usage. Commentary marked C provides tutorial or advisory text to clarify the definitions.
sections.eli5: Every definition has a label: I means use this in standards, N means use this if you must (but it's from somewhere else), O means this is background info, and D means don't use this word. C sections are just extra explanation.

sections.title: Major Security Concepts
sections.content:
The glossary organizes security terminology across several major domains. Cryptographic algorithms include symmetric ciphers (DES, 3DES, IDEA, RC2, Blowfish), asymmetric algorithms (RSA, Diffie-Hellman), hash functions (MD2, MD4, MD5, SHA-1), and modes of operation (CBC, ECB, CFB).

Authentication and access control cover mechanisms such as passwords, digital signatures, biometric authentication, and access control models (mandatory access control, discretionary access control). Key management encompasses key agreement, key transport, key establishment protocols, and key validation. Internet protocols include IPsec protocols (ISAKMP, IKE, AH, ESP), TLS, X.509 certificates, and public-key infrastructure (PKI) concepts. Security attacks and vulnerabilities range from passive eavesdropping to active attacks like man-in-the-middle, masquerading, and denial of service. Security models and policies describe formal frameworks like the Bell-LaPadula model and terminology for classifying information (Top Secret, Secret, etc.).
sections.eli5: The glossary covers the main topics in computer security: how to scramble data (encryption), how to prove who you are (authentication), how to share secret keys, how protocols protect networks, what attacks look like, and how to organize who can access what.

sections.title: Why Terminology Matters
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that consistent terminology is essential for implementing Internet standards correctly. A concrete example illustrates the problem: the term message authentication code (uncapitalized) mixes three distinct concepts: the word message suggests electronic mail, authentication suggests proof of identity, and code suggests encryption or software. In reality, the mechanism is primarily a checksum (data integrity protection), not true authentication. RFC 2828 recommends using specific terms like checksum, keyed hash, or protected checksum instead, depending on the exact function needed.

Another deprecated term is malware, which RFC 2828 recommends against because it is not in most dictionaries and could confuse international readers who are unfamiliar with English-language contractions. The preferred term is malicious software or malicious logic.

The RFC also warns against proprietary or vendor-favoring terms, and terms that might bias standards toward one security technology over competing alternatives. By promoting neutral, well-established language, the glossary helps ensure that Internet standards remain fair, implementable, and internationally understandable.
sections.eli5: Using the right word matters because a wrong word can confuse programmers or make them implement the wrong thing. For example, saying message authentication code makes people think about email when they should think about checking if data got scrambled during transfer.

sections.title: Examples and References
sections.content:
The glossary includes extensive references to authoritative sources, including Internet RFCs, U.S. government standards (such as FIPS and NSA documents), international standards (ITU-T, ISO), and industry specifications (such as X.509 and SET). For example, the entry for Bell-LaPadula Model includes a formal definition and explains the three key properties: the confinement property (controlling write access), the simple security property (controlling read access), and the tranquility property (controlling when classifications change).

The RFC also explains practical contexts. For instance, back door is marked as an I-definition and includes a note that operating systems sometimes ship with privileged accounts for vendor maintenance, clarifying that back doors do not necessarily indicate malicious intent. Similarly, the entry on bastion host explains how firewalls use a single strongly protected host to minimize the attack surface, and notes that some services like DNS have forwarding built in, while others like Telnet require a proxy.
sections.eli5: The glossary gives examples to show how terms work. It explains what a firewall bastion host is (one extra-protected computer that blocks outside attacks) and why companies might deliberately leave back doors in systems (for maintenance, not just for spies).

sections.title: Supporting Standards Process Goals
sections.content:
RFC 2828 explicitly supports four goals of the Internet Standards Process: Clear, Concise, and Easily Understood Documentation (by establishing consistent terminology), Technical Excellence (by using terminology accurately and unambiguously), Prior Implementation and Testing (by using well-established language and avoiding made-up terms), and Openness, Fairness, and Timeliness (by avoiding proprietary or vendor-biased terms and remaining flexible as security technology evolves).

The RFC acknowledges that it is not itself a standard and that its recommendations represent the author's best judgment, based on the need for clear communication in the Internet community. The document notes that terms differ between standards bodies (such as the American Bar Association, OSI, SET, and the U.S. Department of Defense), and the glossary attempts to use understandable English that does not contradict any single authority while promoting a shared, neutral vocabulary across all Internet standards.
sections.eli5: The goal is to help Internet standards be clear, correct, and fair. By using common words instead of brand names or made-up terms, standards work better and everyone understands them the same way.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 2828 was published in May 2000 as an Informational document (FYI 36). It remains an Internet Standard and is still widely cited as a reference for security terminology. However, the security field evolved significantly after 2000, and RFC 4949, published in August 2007, replaces RFC 2828 with expanded and updated definitions reflecting advances in cryptography, protocols, and threat models.

RFC 2828 established a durable model for maintaining shared terminology in security standards, demonstrating that consistent language is as important as correct protocol design for standards that people must implement correctly. The RFC's insistence on avoiding ambiguous or misleading terms remains relevant today, as security terminology continues to evolve with new threats, new standards, and new technologies.
sections.eli5: This glossary was the definitive security dictionary from 2000 to 2007. It was then updated (RFC 4949) because security changed a lot. The idea behind it—that everyone needs to use the same words—is still true today.
